This new feature mirrors the famous hexagonal wave at Saturn's north pole, which has persisted for over 40 years; the south pole's tilt away from Earth prevented observations until recently.

Lead author Agustin Sanchez-Lavega of the University of the Basque Country credited amateur astronomers alongside Hubble Space Telescope data in identifying the decagon, which moves at roughly 10 kilometers per hour within a jet stream reaching 400 kilometers per hour.

Comparing these two polar formations allows scientists to better understand atmospheric dynamics on gas giants. Researchers are analyzing whether the decagon is a stable structure or a transient phenomenon driven by atmospheric disturbances.

Future observations by the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes will determine if the decagon evolves into a robust feature or dissipates. Unlike the stationary northern hexagon, the decagon's vertices shift, raising questions about its long-term stability.

summary: On Wednesday, CHIRLA filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration , alleging the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and Attorney General Todd Blanche illegally target naturalized citizens to prevent them from voting.

Following an executive order titled 'Ensuring Citizenship and Integrity in Federal Elections' signed by President Donald Trump in March, the White House claims over 278,000 non-citizens are registered nationwide, including 190,000 in California.

UCLA Voting Rights Projects Senior Data Scientist Michael Rios warned that comparing databases without unique identifiers produces errors, stating, 'Unless databases have a unique identifier to merge them by, a similar name, birthdate, or address cannot establish that two records represent the same person.'

Plaintiff Pedro Trujillo, a naturalized citizen, joined the lawsuit to oppose 'voter intimidation' and fears the administration is 'creating second-class citizenship where naturalized citizens are not given the rights they have earned.'

While the Center for Election Innovation & Research reports non-citizen voting is 'extremely small,' DHS maintains it is 'laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote,' despite critics arguing such claims represent less than one-tenth of one percent of registered voters.
title: Immigrant rights group seeks to block use of federal databases it says could purge legal voters

bias: Left-Leaning coverage foregrounds Pauken’s claimed motive—“preventing World War III” rather than “betraying America”—while right-leaning accounts stress punishment, alleged “American secrets,” paid espionage , and China’s Ministry of State Security, even placing “journalist” in scare quotes and invoking a “communist country.” The center framing de-emphasizes motive and emphasizes the guilty plea, “spying for China,” arrest, and state-media ties.
The pivotal divide is whether his conduct is interpreted through intent and antiwar belief or through betrayal, national-security risk, and possible Chinese influence.
All perspectives acknowledge the two-year sentence and China connection, reflecting wider tensions over loyalty, foreign interference, and U.S.-China rivalry.
summary: On Tuesday, Thomas Pauken II, an American journalist, was sentenced to two years in prison for acting as an unregistered agent for the Chinese government while living in Beijing.
Prosecutors charged that Pauken accepted $100,000 over seven years to write reports on U.S.-Chinese relations that were conveyed to Chinese leaders, including Chinese President Xi Jinping .
FBI agents arrested Pauken in Washington last winter after he attempted to recruit a Trump administration official for a Chinese handler, despite a 2025 FBI warning.
Judge Leonie Brinkema ordered Pauken to undergo three years of supervised release with no overseas travel, while acknowledging the 'very unfortunate' situation affecting his family.
Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg stated the Justice Department remains committed to holding accountable anyone who aids Chinese espionage efforts.
title: A US Journalist Sentenced to 2 Years in Federal Prison for Acting as an Illegal Agent for China

summary: On Wednesday, Maryland District Judge Deborah Boardman blocked President Donald Trump's latest executive order limiting birthright citizenship , granting a preliminary injunction to immigrant rights advocates.
This ruling follows the Supreme Court's rejection of Trump's initial 2025 effort, which the administration sought to revive through an August 6 order targeting 'birth tourism.'
Boardman called the directive 'almost certainly unconstitutional,' noting it contradicts the 14th Amendment and the high court's recent ruling that children born in the United States are citizens.
The injunction protects babies represented by the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project and CASA, ensuring their citizenship status remains honored while litigation continues.
Justice Department attorneys previously argued the lawsuit was premature, as federal agencies have yet to issue public implementation guidance expected by September 5.
title: A judge blocks Trump’s new bid to curb birthright citizenship, citing Supreme Court precedent

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Trump’s tour as selective and conflict-ridden, using terms like “snubs GOP leaders,” “vulnerable seats,” and “sagging popularity,” especially highlighting his refusal to campaign for figures such as Mike Johnson.

Right-Leaning coverage instead emphasizes momentum and party-building: “a lot of stops,” a “30-day campaign tour,” support for governors, and a “winning midterm message,” while portraying his record as a viable electoral asset.
Center coverage presents the travel as an extensive effort targeting “high-stakes races” that could determine congressional control.
All acknowledge the roughly 30-day schedule, numerous contests, and reliance on Trump’s record, reflecting broader divides over leadership, loyalty, and electoral strength.
summary: On Wednesday, President Donald Trump announced plans to spend the final 30 days before November's midterm elections traveling to about 35 battleground states to support Republican candidates for the House and Senate.

Republicans face a challenging midterm season with slim majorities, prompting Trump to encourage vulnerable lawmakers to run on his record and reverse historical patterns where presidents lose midterm races.
Trump told House Speaker Mike Johnson and other secure GOP leaders not to request campaign visits if leading by 40 points, saying, 'Please don't ask me to come to your area and make a speech.'

In Alaska, Trump pledged support for Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, while in Texas he praised Attorney General Ken Paxton as 'the best attorney general in the country,' despite Paxton's scandal-plagued past.
The campaign push arrives as a Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump's approval rating at 33%, his lowest ever, while Republicans contend with voter concerns over the economy and international tensions.
title: Trump Promises to Campaign for Republicans and Says They Have a Winning Midterm Message

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Ben-Gvir’s entry as “storms,” “invasion,” “desecration,” and “Judaization,” foregrounding Hamas and Jordan’s accusations of an “unacceptable provocation” and international-law violation.

Right-Leaning coverage de-emphasizes those consequences, emphasizing police protection, guards, and Israeli civilians, while still using “far-right” and “storms,” revealing limited ideological defense.

The pivotal divide is whether the visit signifies occupation and religious erasure or a security-managed ministerial appearance.

summary: On Monday, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in East Jerusalem , performing prayers and declaring plans to alter the historical status quo of Islam's third-holiest site.
The Jewish Power party leader has repeatedly entered the compound since taking office in 2022, consistently advocating for taking over the site to build a Jewish temple instead.

During the incursion, Ben-Gvir stated, "we must bring the prayer incantations and blow the shofar," according to Al Jazeera Arabic's Elias Karram, violating the 1967 status quo prohibiting non-Muslim prayer.
The Jerusalem governorate condemned the incursion as a "dangerous escalation" and flagrant violation attempting to "alter its Islamic identity," according to Wafa.

Israeli police permit daily settler incursions excluding Fridays and Saturdays, while restrictions limit Palestinian worshippers—only 10,000 from the 3.3 million West Bank population accessed Al-Aqsa during Ramadan this year.
title: Far-Right Israeli Minister Storms Al-Aqsa Mosque Under Police Protection

summary: U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani hears arguments Thursday on whether to extend a prohibition against the U.S. Postal Service requiring states to use a new mail-balloting system mandated by President Donald Trump .

Trump's March executive order directed federal agencies to create citizenship lists, limiting mail ballots to those voters. The administration contends the changes are legal, while opponents argue the president lacks constitutional authority to set election rules.

After receiving a whistleblower report, Senator Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., raised concerns that the Postal Service's system could cause millions of ballots to go unsent. "We need to safeguard the right to vote," Blumenthal said.

North Carolina begins shipping mail ballots to voters on Friday, a day after the Boston hearing. The Supreme Court previously ruled a challenge to the Postal Service directive was premature, though the administration's order expires next week.

Separately, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Washington alleging databases target naturalized citizens. These legal challenges could significantly impact November elections in states where mail-in voting predominates, including California and Colorado.
title: Federal Judge Considers Whether to Extend Ban Against US Postal Service Mail Voting Changes

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Hochul’s hijab as cultural solidarity and Trump’s response as “attacking” her appearance through “Islamophobic speech and hatred,” while right-leaning coverage portrays the gesture as “cosplaying” or an effort to “pander for votes,” amplified by its timing before 9/11 and an Iranian dissident’s comparison with women’s oppression in Iran.

The left uses moralized language defending Muslims; the right favors combative terms such as “torpedoes,” “blistering broadside,” “worst governor,” and “crazy.” Center coverage de-emphasizes those ideological stakes, presenting “backlash” and the Hochul-Blakeman exchange as a dispute.
All agree she wore the hijab and Trump criticized it, revealing broader divides over Islamophobia, multicultural symbolism, national security, and political authenticity.
summary: Governor Kathy Hochul wore a hijab during a visit to a mosque in Queens, which sparked backlash from critics including President Donald Trump and Bruce Blakeman.
Hochul defended her actions by stating she was a guest at a Muslim place of worship and refused to apologize for treating people of any faith with dignity.
Iranian exile Sana Ebrahimi Ledene criticized Hochul for wearing a hijab, highlighting the oppression Iranian women face under Tehran's regime for refusing to wear it.
title: Gov. Kathy Hochul responds to backlash from Bruce Blakeman over hijab controversy

Center coverage de-emphasizes those implications, briefly reporting that he “mocks” a friend taking such medication.

summary: On Wednesday, President Donald Trump spoke at a Rose Garden dinner, making comments about an "obese" friend and claiming he told the individual, "you look like ."
Trump recounted telling the friend, "I said, you're an extremely obese person," noting the individual begged him not to reveal his name because he'd "destroy his reputation."

Social media users speculated about the friend's identity, with Jackie Singh referencing Trump's communications director Steven Cheung, who has reportedly been on the receiving end of Trump's fat-shaming before.
Liberal commentator Vince Wilson suggested, "Trump is talking about himself. Piggy was looking in the mirror," while Meidas Touch posted, "Checking in on Trump's midterm messaging."
Patriot Takes wrote, "What a crazy time line we live in," while reporter Aaron Rupar added, "Your mileage may vary," reflecting broader bewilderment at the president's comments.
title: Trump Faces Criticism After Admitting Insulting Overweight Friend

bias: Left-Leaning coverage uses “alarmed,” “superstorm,” and “crash” to dramatize a potential public-safety threat from GPS errors exceeding 33 feet, while right-leaning coverage stresses “risk” to autonomous vehicles and precision farming, reflecting skepticism about rapidly adopted automation rather than documenting an accident.
The pivotal divide is whether to foreground catastrophic possibility or technological reliability.
Center coverage adds ionospheric interference, seasonal timing, possible agricultural losses of hundreds of millions during spring planting, detection limits, and spoofing vulnerabilities.
Across perspectives, the shared emphasis is that solar activity disrupted GPS and could endanger autonomous transport and precision agriculture , with disagreement mainly over urgency and context.
summary: On August 29, 2026, researchers published findings in Geophysical Research Letters detailing how a November 2025 geomagnetic storm shifted GPS readings by more than 33 feet, disrupting autonomous vehicles and precision farming across North America.

The November 2025 storm, a severe G4 event classified by NOAA, drove the auroral oval toward the equator, creating intense ionospheric density gradients that pushed radio signals off course across the continental United States and Canada.

Fixed satellite-navigation receivers recorded positioning errors exceeding 10 meters, or 33 feet, during the disturbance. Such deviations render centimeter-level guidance systems used by self-driving cars and automated farm machinery dangerous to operate.

While the November event occurred post-harvest, researchers noted a similar May 2024 Gannon storm struck during planting, costing American farmers roughly $500 million in potential profits. Widespread navigation outages during peak season could trigger comparable economic losses.

The event revealed critical vulnerabilities in mid-latitude regions previously considered safe from space-weather interference. Improved space-weather prediction and physics-based modeling are essential, the study concludes, to reduce future disruptions to autonomous systems and precision agriculture .
title: Study: November Solar Storm Skewed US GPS by 33 Feet

summary: On Wednesday, the DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge over the Chicago River became stuck in the "up" position following a 10 a.m. scheduled lift, snarling traffic on the major highway.
Extreme heat caused steel bridge components to expand, preventing the two bridge leaves from fully closing, according to Erica Schroeder, a spokesperson for the Chicago Department of Transportation.
A Chicago Fire Department fireboat sprayed water across the 200-foot steel span to cool the metal, while police redirected Downtown traffic after the malfunction caused significant backups.
After crews completed adjustments, the bridge lowered and reopened to traffic shortly before 2:30 p.m. Wednesday, according to Schroeder.
Chicago remains under a heat advisory through Wednesday night, with the National Weather Service forecasting "feels like" temperatures as high as 105 degrees.
title: Popular downtown Chicago bridge stuck in up position due to heat

bias: Coverage largely agrees that Thomas Fahmy was struck by lightning near his car in Staten Island, captured on video, hospitalized, and discharged without major visible burns, but its framing diverges: left-leaning accounts emphasize pain, numbness, overnight monitoring, a “good samaritan,” and Fahmy’s later church visit, presenting a textured survival story; right-leaning accounts foreground him as a “GOP staffer,” call the survival “incredible” or “miraculously” achieved, and highlight “Thank you, God,” adding partisan and providential meaning while stressing he walked away “without a scratch.” Center coverage de-emphasizes politics , instead using “terrifying,” “jaw-dropping,” or “miraculous” to heighten spectacle.
The divide reflects broader tensions over partisan identity, religion, and emotional interpretation, despite shared emphasis on survival.
summary: On Thursday, August 27, Thomas Fahmy, a congressional staffer for Representative Nicole Malliotakis, was struck by lightning while walking on Staten Island, New York. Surveillance footage captured the moment he was hit.

Walking 15 to 25 feet from his car during gloomy weather, Fahmy was struck by the bolt and dropped to the ground. He described the experience as an "intense burning sensation. Tingling, numbness, pain, severe pain, in both my feet."
Transported to Staten Island University Hospital, Fahmy was monitored overnight for potential injuries. He avoided serious burns or major trauma and was discharged the following day.
Representative Nicole Malliotakis expressed relief, stating, "We are happy, grateful and relieved that Thomas is alive and well." She thanked the good Samaritan and medical staff for emergency care.

The National Weather Service explained that direct lightning strikes are less common but remain the most deadly. In most strikes, current travels via "flashover" over skin or through cardiovascular and nervous systems.
title: Congressional aide survives lightning strike in New York

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the 89% figure—up 10 points to a 20-year high—as “sprawling” or “rampant” corruption and a “deepening crisis of confidence,” linking it to Trump’s return and institutional decline.

Right-Leaning coverage stresses “public distrust” but highlights “bipartisan convergence,” noting concern among Democrats , independents , and Republicans , while sometimes adding international comparisons.
Center coverage de-emphasizes blame, presenting a record-setting perception rather than verified misconduct.

The pivotal divide is whether the poll signals Trump-linked crisis or cross-party rejection of government; all emphasize unprecedented distrust, revealing broader disputes over leadership, institutions, and partisan responsibility.
summary: Gallup released survey data Wednesday showing 89% of Americans believe government corruption is widespread, marking a 10-point increase from last year and the highest level recorded in two decades.

Perception shifts are driven largely by Democrats and independents, with 91% and 90% respectively reporting corruption, while 83% of Republicans share that view, representing a significant departure from 2010–2025 norms.

For the first time, the United States leads the 38-member Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development in perceived corruption, diverging from international trends where median perception levels remain below 60%.

Political scientist David Szakonyi of George Washington University told The Washington Post there is a "broad base consensus for the fact that something is broken in Washington," reflecting rare bipartisan agreement.
Beyond federal concerns, 71% of Americans now consider the U.S. business sector corrupt, an 18-point increase from last year, suggesting skepticism extends across institutional sectors.
title: Perceptions of government corruption at record high: Gallup

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Bessent’s attribution as morally and politically offensive, using terms like “Gross,” “Fury,” “chiding,” and “Trump’s Minister,” while stressing Russia’s invasion and Ukraine’s strategy to weaken Moscow’s war financing.

Right-Leaning coverage instead portrays Ukrainian strikes as a “root cause” of global instability, highlights efforts to lower prices “at the pump,” and suggests the administration is “courting Russia” before midterms.

Center coverage qualifies Ukraine’s role as “partly” contributing to an “energy shock.” All emphasize the strikes, rising prices, and intertwined wars, revealing divides over accountability, Ukraine policy, and Trump-era diplomacy.
summary: On Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for creating a global "energy shock" and contributing to rising fuel prices worldwide.

Speaking at the G20 meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, Bessent conceded "prices are too high" while also identifying the conflict with Iran in the Strait of Hormuz as a factor impacting energy markets.
Bessent noted that "the bottom 25% of wage earners' wages went up 4.7%" and highlighted Chevron's $7 billion investment in Venezuela as evidence of economic relief efforts.

The remarks drew swift backlash from analysts; Max Boot accused Bessent of "literally blaming the victim," while CNN chief national security analyst Jim Sciutto questioned if the administration aims to save Russian industry.

Critics including Nicolas Tenzer and The Dispatch's Jonah Goldberg argued the administration's stance repeats narratives favorable to the Kremlin, potentially undermining efforts to restrict Vladimir Putin's ability to fund his invasion.
title: Bessent partly blames Ukraine for ‘energy shock’ pushing up prices
